Coding Assignment 1: Restaurant Sales and Daily Maximum Temperature

Author

Seth Johnson and Rachel Wiggins

Published

September 29, 2026

Purpose

The purpose of this assignment is to give you an opportunity to apply many of the data assembly concepts that you have learned about in this course.

Objectives

The main objective of this assignment is to explore whether restaurant sales are associated with daily maximum temperatures. However, the data come from different data frames that need to be restructured so that the data in them can be joined together.

  • Work with your teammates to complete the tasks.
  • Use several data assembly tasks, including those listed below:
    • Reading in data from Parquet files
    • Dealing with rows that have missing values
    • Reshaping data frames
    • Creating new columns in a data frame
    • Joining data frames
  • Perform some initial exploration of the data in a data frame.
  • Practice using tidyverse functions to clean, reshape, summarize, join, and visualize data.

Task

Work with your assigned team to complete this coding assignment using R, Quarto, and tidyverse. Your goal is to explore whether restaurant sales are associated with daily maximum temperatures by cleaning, reshaping, and joining two datasets:

  • ities.parquet
  • max_temp.parquet

Download both Parquet files from Canvas and save them in the same folder as your Quarto (.qmd) file.

Begin by creating a new Quarto document (.qmd) in RStudio or Positron. Follow the step-by-step instructions to import data, handle missing values, reshape data frames, and generate summary statistics. You will also create new columns, join datasets, and produce visualizations to explore relationships between variables.

Once you have completed all required tasks, restart your R session, render the entire document, and make sure the HTML file is created without errors.

Quick Render Check

Run the code below and render your Quarto document.
If the plot appears in the HTML file, your document is rendering R output correctly.

plot(
  cars,
  main = "Quarto Render Check",
  xlab = "Speed",
  ylab = "Stopping Distance"
)

Include code that displays the count of missing values in each column of dfi.

Note that only a small number of rows are affected, and not every column contains missing values.

Use tidyverse functions such as summarise() and across() where appropriate.

Choose to remove the rows with missing values or impute the missing values, and then use appropriate commands to complete that process.

#price is 12.02 for Beef and Squash Kabob

#replacing Price values using case_when, TRUE leaves other values untouched
dfi_cleaned <- dfi %>%
  mutate(Price = case_when(
    Category == "Chicken" & is.na(Price) ~ 14.68,
    Category == "Beef" & is.na(Price) ~ 12.02,
    TRUE ~ Price
  ))

#replacing TotalDue with calculated values from Price and Quantity
dfi_real_clean <- dfi_cleaned %>%
  mutate(TotalDue = case_when(
    Category == "Chicken" & is.na(TotalDue) ~ 14.68 * Quantity,
    Category == "Beef" & is.na(TotalDue) ~ 12.02 * Quantity,
    TRUE ~ Price
  ))

#rechecking for missing values
na_counts_dplyr <- dfi %>%
  summarise_all(~ sum(is.na(.)))

7. (8 points) Aggregate the restaurant data to the daily level

We need to prepare dfi and dfw so that we can join them together.

To do so, we want to aggregate the restaurant data at the daily level.

Create a new data frame named dfid by aggregating dfi at the daily level.

The data frame dfid must contain the date column and the columns Quantity and TotalDue from dfi, summarized at the daily level.

Use tidyverse functions such as:

  • group_by()
  • summarise()

Include code that displays the first 10 rows of dfid to verify that it worked.

In 1–2 sentences, defend the choice of the summary measure (sum, mean, or another measure) used to aggregate the values in each column.

dfid <- dfi_real_clean %>%
  group_by(Date) %>%
  summarize(
    Quantity= sum(Quantity, na.rm = TRUE), 
    TotalDue = sum(TotalDue, na.rm = TRUE)
    )

head(dfid, n=10)

Aggregating by sum seemed like a good way to visualize differences in how much money was brought in per day. Taking the average would give the average quantity and total due per transaction, and that doesn’t seem to be what we are interested in.

8. (4 points) Reshape the weather data

Create a new data frame named dfwd by converting dfw from a wide format to a long format.

The names of the seven columns, Monday through Sunday, should be stored in a new column named day, and the values from those seven columns should be stored in a new column named max_temp.

Use the tidyverse function pivot_longer().

Include code that displays the first 10 rows of dfwd to verify that the conversion worked.

# converting to long format
dfwd <- dfw %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = Monday:Sunday, names_to = "day", values_to = "max_temp")

9. (8 points) Create a Date column

Update the dfwd data frame by adding a column named Date that corresponds to the value in the day column.

Each WeekStarting value is the Sunday on which that week begins, so the Monday of that week is the day after WeekStarting, and the Sunday at the end of that week is seven days after WeekStarting.

For example, if the WeekStarting value is 2016-01-03, then the value in the Date column for the Monday that comes after 2016-01-03 should be 2016-01-04.

Use tidyverse functions such as mutate() and case_when() where appropriate.

Arrange dfwd in ascending order of Date and include code to display the first 10 rows to verify that it worked.

Beneath the output, comment on how you know that the creation of the Date column worked.

# Calcualting dates
dfwd <- dfwd %>% 
  mutate(Date = case_when(
    day == "Sunday" ~ WeekStarting,
    day == "Monday" ~ WeekStarting + 1, 
    day == "Tuesday" ~ WeekStarting + 2, 
    day == "Wednesday" ~ WeekStarting + 3, 
    day == "Thursday" ~ WeekStarting + 4, 
    day == "Friday" ~ WeekStarting + 5, 
    day == "Saturday" ~ WeekStarting + 6,
    TRUE ~ as.Date(NA)
  ))

dfwd <- dfwd %>% 
   arrange(Date)

10. (4 points) Join the two data frames

Join the data frames dfid and dfwd into one data frame named df such that only the rows that are in both dfid and dfwd are included in df.

Use the tidyverse function inner_join().

Arrange df in ascending order of Date.

Then include code that displays something to show that the join worked.

Briefly identify how that output helps you know that the join worked.

The restaurant data and the weather data do not cover the same span of dates, so df will have far fewer rows than dfid. As a check on your work, df should contain 311 rows. If your row count differs, revisit your date conversions in Task 4 and your Date column in Task 9.

In 1–2 sentences, explain why an inner join is the appropriate choice here, and identify what would have been different had you used left_join() instead.

# inner join by date column
df <- inner_join(dfid, dfwd, by = "Date")

df <- df %>%
  arrange(Date)

dim(df)

11. (8 points) Create scatterplots

Use ggplot2 to create the three scatterplots described below.

Make sure each plot has an appropriate title and clearly labeled axes.

A. Maximum temperature and TotalDue

Create a scatterplot with:

  • max_temp on the x-axis
  • TotalDue on the y-axis
# Plotting max temp and total due
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(df, aes(x = max_temp, y = TotalDue)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum temp and Total Due",
    x = "Max Temp",
    y = "Total Due"
  )
B. Maximum temperature and Quantity

Create a scatterplot with:

  • max_temp on the x-axis
  • Quantity on the y-axis
# plotting max temp and quantity sold
ggplot(df, aes(x = max_temp, y = Quantity)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum temp and Quantity",
    x = "Max Temp",
    y = "Quantity"
  )
C. Quantity and TotalDue

Create a scatterplot with:

  • Quantity on the x-axis
  • TotalDue on the y-axis
# plotting quantity sold and total amount due
ggplot(df, aes(x = Quantity, y = TotalDue)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Qunatity and total Due",
    x = "Quantity",
    y = "Total Due"
  )

Below the third scatterplot, identify whether there appears to be a relationship for each pair of variables:

  • max_temp and TotalDue
  • max_temp and Quantity
  • Quantity and TotalDue

For each relationship, briefly describe the direction, form, and strength of the pattern you observe.

Remember that these are observational data, so the scatterplots can show an association but do not by themselves establish causation.

Interpretation:

The scatterplot of max_temp plotted against TotalDue appears to show data oriented horizontally, with fairly consistent variance, with an intercept just above 5000. The fact that the line is horizontal, the data homoscedastic, and that the errors don’t seem to demonstrate autocorrelation all seem to suggest that there is not a strong relationship between these two variables.

The situation appears to be similar for max_temp and Quantity where the data seems like it could again be adequately modeled with just a horizontal line representing the mean. The quantity does not seem to vary as X (max_temp) varies.

Because the plots of max_tempandTotalDueandmax_tempandQuantityshowed similar shape and variance, it is perhaps unsurprising thatQuantityandTotalDue`appear to be positively associated. The data seems like it could be modeled here with a straight line with a positive slope. Shapewise, the data is gathered downward toward the place a regression line looks like it should go, with the variance stretching only upward. This suggests the relationship between quantity and total due, which, for each product separately would be perfectly linear (total due is an exact number based on quantity.) But this plot includes all products, which explains the variance of data that appears to be floating upwards off the line: some products are more expensive than others, and the more expensive ones are not purchased as often.

## Purpose

The purpose of this assignment is to give you an opportunity to apply many of the data assembly concepts that you have learned about in this course.

### Objectives

The main objective of this assignment is to explore whether restaurant sales are associated with daily maximum temperatures. However, the data come from different data frames that need to be restructured so that the data in them can be joined together.

- Work with your teammates to complete the tasks.
- Use several data assembly tasks, including those listed below:
  - Reading in data from Parquet files
  - Dealing with rows that have missing values
  - Reshaping data frames
  - Creating new columns in a data frame
  - Joining data frames
- Perform some initial exploration of the data in a data frame.
- Practice using `tidyverse` functions to clean, reshape, summarize, join, and visualize data.

### Task

Work with your assigned team to complete this coding assignment using **R, Quarto, and tidyverse**. Your goal is to explore whether restaurant sales are associated with daily maximum temperatures by cleaning, reshaping, and joining two datasets:

- `ities.parquet`
- `max_temp.parquet`

Download both Parquet files from Canvas and save them in the same folder as your Quarto (`.qmd`) file.

Begin by creating a new Quarto document (`.qmd`) in RStudio or Positron. Follow the step-by-step instructions to import data, handle missing values, reshape data frames, and generate summary statistics. You will also create new columns, join datasets, and produce visualizations to explore relationships between variables.

Once you have completed all required tasks, restart your R session, render the entire document, and make sure the HTML file is created without errors.

### Assignment Instructions

#### 1. (2 point) Load the packages

#### 4. (8 points) Check and convert data types

Using any appropriate commands, make any necessary data type conversions to columns in **dfi** and/or **dfw**.

When appropriate, use tidyverse functions such as `mutate()` together with functions for converting dates, numbers, or character variables.

Include code that displays the updated structure of the data frames to verify that the data type conversions, if any, worked.

Below the output, comment on why you did or did not make data type conversions.

You may want to come back to this task and update it once you start working on the subsequent tasks.

```{r}
#| label: q04-convert-data-types

# The date format here is not very effective for analysis. I will update it to convert it to yy-mm-dd

library(lubridate)

head(dfw, 5)

**Comment:**
From looking at the first five rows of each data frame, the date was give in a chr format. chr is not sufficient for analysis, so I knew if we were to use dates in any analysis this will need to be changed.

#### 5. (2 point) Display summary statistics

Display summary statistics for all columns of both data frames.

#| label: q05-summary-statistics

summary(dfi)

```

#### 6. (6 points) Identify and handle missing values

Include code that displays the count of missing values in each column of **dfi**.

Note that only a small number of rows are affected, and not every column contains missing values.

Use tidyverse functions such as `summarise()` and `across()` where appropriate.

Choose to remove the rows with missing values or impute the missing values, and then use appropriate commands to complete that process.

Use code to display evidence that it worked, such as summarizing the missing values again.

Defend that choice in 1–2 sentences for each column with missing values.

```{r}
#| label: q06-missing-values


library(dplyr)

# finding rows with missing values in dfi
na_counts_dplyr <- dfi %>%
  summarise_all(~ sum(is.na(.)))


print(na_counts_dplyr)


# Display rows where columns contain NA
dfi_missing <- dfi %>%
  filter(if_any(everything(), is.na))

print(dfi_missing)

#missing prices come from Price and TotalDue columns

#finding price values of Chicken and Onion Kabob and Beef and Squash Kabob

chick_onion <- dfi %>%
  filter(LineItem == "Chicken and Onion Kabob")

head(chick_onion)

#price is 14.68 for Chicken and Onion Kabob

#finding price values of Beef and Squash Kabob

beef_squash <- dfi %>%
  filter(LineItem == "Beef and Squash Kabob")

head(beef_squash)

#price is 12.02 for Beef and Squash Kabob

#replacing Price values using case_when, TRUE leaves other values untouched
dfi_cleaned <- dfi %>%
  mutate(Price = case_when(
    Category == "Chicken" & is.na(Price) ~ 14.68,
    Category == "Beef" & is.na(Price) ~ 12.02,
    TRUE ~ Price
  ))

#replacing TotalDue with calculated values from Price and Quantity
dfi_real_clean <- dfi_cleaned %>%
  mutate(TotalDue = case_when(
    Category == "Chicken" & is.na(TotalDue) ~ 14.68 * Quantity,
    Category == "Beef" & is.na(TotalDue) ~ 12.02 * Quantity,
    TRUE ~ Price
  ))

#rechecking for missing values
na_counts_dplyr <- dfi %>%
  summarise_all(~ sum(is.na(.)))

summary(dfi_real_clean)

```


**Explanation:**

It seems logical, since the missing values were price values, to fill missing Price values in with information from other rows with the same product. Then it's just a simple matter of doing a simple calculation to complete the TotalDue column. 

#### 7. (8 points) Aggregate the restaurant data to the daily level

We need to prepare **dfi** and **dfw** so that we can join them together.

To do so, we want to aggregate the restaurant data at the daily level.

Create a new data frame named **dfid** by aggregating **dfi** at the daily level.

The data frame **dfid** must contain the date column and the columns `Quantity` and `TotalDue` from **dfi**, summarized at the daily level.

Use tidyverse functions such as:

- `group_by()`
- `summarise()`

Include code that displays the first 10 rows of **dfid** to verify that it worked.

In 1–2 sentences, defend the choice of the summary measure (sum, mean, or another measure) used to aggregate the values in each column.

```{r}
#| label: q07-aggregate-daily

dfid <- dfi_real_clean %>%
  group_by(Date) %>%
  summarize(
    Quantity= sum(Quantity, na.rm = TRUE), 
    TotalDue = sum(TotalDue, na.rm = TRUE)
    )

head(dfid, n=10)

```

**Explanation:**

Aggregating by sum seemed like a good way to visualize differences in how much money was brought in per day. Taking the average would give the average quantity and total due per transaction, and that doesn't seem to be what we are interested in. 

#### 8. (4 points) Reshape the weather data

Create a new data frame named **dfwd** by converting **dfw** from a wide format to a long format.

The names of the seven columns, Monday through Sunday, should be stored in a new column named `day`, and the values from those seven columns should be stored in a new column named `max_temp`.

Use the tidyverse function `pivot_longer()`.

Include code that displays the first 10 rows of **dfwd** to verify that the conversion worked.

```{r}
#| label: q08-reshape-weather

# converting to long format
dfwd <- dfw %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = Monday:Sunday, names_to = "day", values_to = "max_temp")


head(dfwd, n=10)
  
```

#### 9. (8 points) Create a Date column

Update the **dfwd** data frame by adding a column named `Date` that corresponds to the value in the `day` column.

Each `WeekStarting` value is the **Sunday** on which that week begins, so the Monday of that week is the day *after* `WeekStarting`, and the Sunday at the end of that week is seven days after `WeekStarting`.

For example, if the `WeekStarting` value is `2016-01-03`, then the value in the `Date` column for the Monday that comes after `2016-01-03` should be `2016-01-04`.

Use tidyverse functions such as `mutate()` and `case_when()` where appropriate.

Arrange **dfwd** in ascending order of `Date` and include code to display the first 10 rows to verify that it worked.

Beneath the output, comment on how you know that the creation of the `Date` column worked.

```{r}
#| label: q09-create-date

# Calcualting dates
dfwd <- dfwd %>% 
  mutate(Date = case_when(
    day == "Sunday" ~ WeekStarting,
    day == "Monday" ~ WeekStarting + 1, 
    day == "Tuesday" ~ WeekStarting + 2, 
    day == "Wednesday" ~ WeekStarting + 3, 
    day == "Thursday" ~ WeekStarting + 4, 
    day == "Friday" ~ WeekStarting + 5, 
    day == "Saturday" ~ WeekStarting + 6,
    TRUE ~ as.Date(NA)
  ))

dfwd <- dfwd %>% 
   arrange(Date)

head(dfwd, n=10)


```

**Comment:**

The creation of the Date column worked because we can see when we look at the first few rows that we now have a new column called Date that has been added to the df

#### 10. (4 points) Join the two data frames

Join the data frames **dfid** and **dfwd** into one data frame named **df** such that only the rows that are in both **dfid** and **dfwd** are included in **df**.

Use the tidyverse function `inner_join()`.

Arrange **df** in ascending order of `Date`.

Then include code that displays something to show that the join worked.

Briefly identify how that output helps you know that the join worked.

The restaurant data and the weather data do not cover the same span of dates, so **df** will have far fewer rows than **dfid**. As a check on your work, **df** should contain **311 rows**. If your row count differs, revisit your date conversions in Task 4 and your `Date` column in Task 9.

In 1–2 sentences, explain why an inner join is the appropriate choice here, and identify what would have been different had you used `left_join()` instead.

```{r}
#| label: q10-join-data

# inner join by date column
df <- inner_join(dfid, dfwd, by = "Date")

df <- df %>%
  arrange(Date)

dim(df)
head(df)


```

**Comment:**
Inner join will keep only data where there is a match from both data frames. If we were to use left join, then everything is kept from the data frame on the left if it had a match or not. In this case we would have to run
analysis again to determine what is missing, and what to do with it. That was already previously done and should not have to be repeated. 
Write your response here.
